topic: Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems: RLS, PII, encryption, audit trails
why: An FDE is usually the person who puts a customer's data into an AI system for the first time, and the customer's security team will not let a pilot touch production data until someone shows them, table by table, how tenant A cannot read tenant B, where PII lives, how it is encrypted and who can prove what was accessed. Application-layer `WHERE tenant_id = ?` filters fail the moment an engineer forgets one, an LLM-generated query bypasses the ORM, or a background job runs as the wrong principal; Postgres row-level security, pgcrypto and an append-only audit log move those guarantees into the database where a reviewer can actually verify them. The schema you design in week one is the schema that survives the handover, so getting isolation, PII handling and auditability right before the first customer row lands is the cheapest security work you will ever do.
prerequisites: PostgreSQL fundamentals from 'PostgreSQL at depth' (topic 29): EXPLAIN ANALYZE, B-tree and composite indexes, transactions and isolation levels, `SET ROLE`, and reading `pg_catalog` views

Auth model from 'Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims' (topic 27): where `tenant_id` and `sub` come from in a verified JWT and why the database must never trust a tenant id the client supplied in a body or query string

FastAPI dependency injection and request lifecycle from topic 26 (or the Next.js route-handler and server-action equivalent for DefenderMate) so you can set per-request session state at the exact point the connection is checked out

IAM and KMS basics from topic 15: what a KMS key policy is, `kms:Decrypt` versus `kms:GenerateDataKey`, and why the application role must never hold both the ciphertext store and unrestricted key access
Docker Compose with a local Postgres 16 container and psql, plus a pytest (or Vitest) harness that can open two connections as different roles inside one test
A written list of every table in DefenderMate today, which columns hold customer-supplied free text, and who (human or service) reads each one

subtopics.name: Choosing the tenancy model: shared schema, schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant
subtopics.learn: Lay out the three isolation models with their real costs: pooled (one schema, `tenant_id` on every row, RLS enforces isolation), bridge (schema-per-tenant with `search_path` switching and N copies of every migration), and silo (database or cluster per tenant, hard isolation, N connection pools and N backups). Know the questions that decide it: does the customer's security policy require physical separation or a dedicated encryption key per tenant, how many tenants will exist in 18 months, does any tenant need a different region for residency, and can you afford per-tenant migrations at 3 a.m. Be able to defend pooled-with-RLS as the default for an AI product with hundreds of small tenants, and name the two triggers (a regulated customer demanding a dedicated key or region; one tenant at 100x the load of the rest) that move a specific tenant to a silo while the others stay pooled.

resource.label: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens (tenant isolation and data partitioning)

subtopics.name: Tenant key discipline: tenant_id on every row and composite foreign keys
subtopics.learn: Every tenant-owned table gets `tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id)` and a `UNIQUE (tenant_id, id)` constraint, and every child table references its parent with a composite `FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, parent_id) REFERENCES parent (tenant_id, id)` so a row cannot point at another tenant's parent even when application code is wrong. Put `tenant_id` first in every index so RLS predicates and tenant-scoped queries show up as `Index Cond` rather than `Filter` in EXPLAIN. Write a catalog query against `information_schema.columns` that lists tables in the `public` schema lacking a `tenant_id` column and run it in CI; the exceptions list (lookup tables, the `tenants` table itself) should be explicit, short and reviewed.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Constraints (composite unique and foreign keys)

subtopics.name: RLS mechanics: ENABLE, FORCE, USING vs WITH CHECK, PERMISSIVE vs RESTRICTIVE
subtopics.learn: Understand exactly what `ALTER TABLE t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` does (default-deny for every role that is not the owner, a superuser or BYPASSRLS) and why you always also run `ALTER TABLE t FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` so the owner is bound too. Write `CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON t FOR ALL TO app_user USING (tenant_id = current_tenant_id()) WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_tenant_id())` and know the asymmetry: `USING` filters rows visible to SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, `WITH CHECK` validates rows produced by INSERT and UPDATE, and a policy with only `USING` lets an UPDATE move a row into another tenant. Know that multiple PERMISSIVE policies are ORed while `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies are ANDed on top, so a second permissive policy added for a 'support can read everything' feature silently widens access to every row; use RESTRICTIVE for hard constraints such as `deleted_at IS NULL` or region pinning.

subtopics.name: Getting the tenant into the session: set_config, current_setting and pooled connections
subtopics.learn: Carry the verified tenant id from the JWT into Postgres with `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)` at the start of every transaction and read it inside policies as `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`; the second argument to `current_setting` is `missing_ok`, which turns an unset variable into NULL (the policy evaluates to NULL, so zero rows) instead of raising. The third argument of `set_config` (`is_local = true`, the equivalent of `SET LOCAL`) scopes the value to the current transaction; with PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode a session-level `SET` leaks the previous tenant to whichever request gets that connection next, which is the single most common cross-tenant bug in pooled RLS deployments. Wrap `set_config` and the business query in one explicit transaction in the repository layer, and add a test that checks out two connections from the pool in sequence and proves the second one sees no tenant.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Configuration Settings Functions (set_config, current_setting)

subtopics.name: Role model: app role without BYPASSRLS, migrator as owner, SECURITY DEFINER escape hatches
subtopics.learn: Create three roles: `app_migrator` owns every object and runs migrations, `app_user` (NOLOGIN, NOBYPASSRLS) is granted to the login role the API uses, and `app_readonly` for analytics gets SELECT on masked views only. Never connect the application as the owner or a superuser; verify with `SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles` in a CI check. When a cross-tenant operation is genuinely required (a system job aggregating usage across tenants), implement it as a `SECURITY DEFINER` function owned by a dedicated role with `SET search_path = pg_catalog, public` in the definition to block search_path hijacking, `REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM PUBLIC`, and a narrow signature that cannot be turned into a generic query runner.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE ROLE (BYPASSRLS, NOLOGIN, INHERIT)

subtopics.name: RLS performance: InitPlan wrapping, LEAKPROOF, and reading EXPLAIN as the app role
subtopics.learn: A policy expression is appended to every query as a predicate, so `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` is evaluated per row unless you write it as `(SELECT current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)`, which the planner turns into a single InitPlan. Understand the leakproof rule: the planner will not push a user-defined or non-`LEAKPROOF` function below the RLS filter (an error message could leak a row), so a `WHERE my_func(col)` that used an index without RLS becomes a sequential scan with it; check `proleakproof` in `pg_proc` and mark trusted immutable functions `LEAKPROOF` only as superuser and only when they cannot throw on any input. Always benchmark with `SET ROLE app_user; SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = ...; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` because the owner or a BYPASSRLS role gets a different plan, and confirm the composite index led by `tenant_id` is the one used.

resource.label: Supabase docs: Row Level Security (RLS performance recommendations)

subtopics.name: The RLS test matrix: positive, negative and privilege-escalation cases per table
subtopics.learn: For every RLS-protected table write at least five tests as the application role: tenant A sees exactly A's rows; tenant B sees zero of A's rows; INSERT with a foreign `tenant_id` fails with `new row violates row-level security policy for table`; UPDATE that changes `tenant_id` to another tenant fails on `WITH CHECK`; DELETE of another tenant's row affects 0 rows and raises no error (silent filtering is RLS behaviour you must document for the client). Add the bypass checks: with no `app.tenant_id` set the count is 0 not an exception; the owner is also filtered because of `FORCE`; and `SET ROLE app_user` cannot then `SET ROLE app_migrator`. Generate the matrix from the catalog (loop over `pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'public'`) so a new table without a policy fails the suite instead of being forgotten, and run it against a real Postgres container in CI, never SQLite or a mock.

subtopics.name: Catalog invariants in CI: pg_policies, relrowsecurity, relforcerowsecurity, event triggers
subtopics.learn: Encode the security posture as queries the pipeline runs after migrations: every table in `public` has `relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity` true in `pg_class` (joined to `pg_namespace`), every such table has at least one row in `pg_policies` for the app role, no role other than the migrator owns any object, and no function referenced from a policy is `SECURITY DEFINER` unless allow-listed. Print the offending table names as the failure message so the reviewer does not have to dig. Optionally add an event trigger `ON ddl_command_end` that inspects `pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands()` and runs `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` on any newly created table in `public`, so an engineer who forgets RLS creates an inaccessible table (a loud failure) rather than an open one.

subtopics.name: PII inventory and classification per column
subtopics.learn: Classify every column as: direct identifier (email, phone, full name, national id), quasi-identifier (postcode, birth date, IP address, device id), special category (health, biometrics, ethnicity, union membership, sexual orientation under GDPR Art. 9), secret (password hash, API key, refresh token), or free text that may contain any of the above (support tickets, chat transcripts, the prompt and completion columns of your AI system). Record the classification, lawful basis, retention period and encryption treatment in one place the security team can read: a `data_inventory` table, or `COMMENT ON COLUMN customers.email IS 'pii:direct;retain:account+30d;enc:column'` parsed by a script into the model doc. The rule for AI systems is that any column an LLM writes to is free text and inherits the highest classification of its inputs.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet: User Privacy Protection

subtopics.name: Encryption layers and pgcrypto: what each layer actually protects against
subtopics.learn: Separate the three layers and the threat each defeats: volume encryption (RDS/EBS with a KMS key) stops a stolen disk or snapshot and nothing else; column encryption with pgcrypto (`pgp_sym_encrypt(text, key)` / `pgp_sym_decrypt(bytea, key)`, or `encrypt(data, key, 'aes-cbc/pad:pkcs')` when you manage IVs yourself) stops a DBA or a leaked `pg_dump` from reading plaintext, but the key is visible in `pg_stat_statements` and server logs if it is passed as a literal; application-layer encryption before the row reaches Postgres stops even the database host from seeing plaintext at the cost of losing SQL search and indexing on that column. Know the pgcrypto footguns: `pgp_sym_encrypt` output is non-deterministic (good for confidentiality, means no equality index), the column type is `bytea`, and keys must travel as bound parameters with `SET LOCAL log_statement = 'none'` for that transaction or they end up in the log.

subtopics.name: Envelope encryption, per-tenant data keys and crypto-shredding
subtopics.learn: Implement the KMS hierarchy: one customer-managed KEK in KMS with a key policy granting the application role `kms:GenerateDataKey` and `kms:Decrypt` only; per tenant, call `GenerateDataKey` once, store the encrypted DEK in `tenants.dek_ciphertext`, cache the plaintext DEK in process memory with a short TTL, and encrypt PII columns with the tenant's DEK using AES-256-GCM with `tenant_id` and the column name as additional authenticated data so a ciphertext copied between rows or tenants fails to decrypt. Rotation is re-wrapping DEKs under the new KEK version, not re-encrypting rows. Crypto-shredding is the payoff: deleting a tenant's DEK (and every copy of it) renders every PII row, backup and replica unreadable, which is how you honour an erasure request without rewriting PITR history; document this as the deletion mechanism in the model doc.

resource.label: AWS KMS Developer Guide: Concepts (envelope encryption, data keys, key policies)

subtopics.name: Searchable PII: HMAC blind indexes, last-four columns, and password hashing
subtopics.learn: You cannot index or filter on a non-deterministic ciphertext, so for each PII column that needs exact lookup (email for login, phone for dedupe) add a sibling `email_hmac bytea` computed as `hmac(lower(trim(email)), :blind_index_key, 'sha256')` with a key different from the encryption key, index that column, and query by HMAC. Understand why a plain `digest(email, 'sha256')` is unacceptable (offline dictionary attack on a low-entropy space like emails) and why per-row salts defeat the purpose (you could no longer look anything up). Store display fragments (`card_last4`, `phone_last2`) as separate plaintext columns rather than decrypting for every list view. For passwords use `crypt(password, gen_salt('bf', 12))` or, better, application-side argon2id; never `pgp_sym_encrypt` a password.

subtopics.name: Masked views, column-level GRANT and security_invoker
subtopics.learn: Give analysts, dashboards and the eval pipeline a redacted surface instead of base tables: `CREATE VIEW customers_masked WITH (security_invoker = true) AS SELECT id, tenant_id, left(email, 1) || '***@' || split_part(email, '@', 2) AS email, ...` so RLS on the base table is evaluated as the querying role (without `security_invoker`, a view runs with the owner's privileges and bypasses RLS). Add `security_barrier = true` when the view filters rows, so a malicious function in the caller's WHERE clause cannot execute before the view's predicate and leak rows through error messages. Use column-level privileges for the reverse case: `GRANT SELECT (id, tenant_id, created_at) ON customers TO app_readonly` lets a role read a table without its PII columns, and `SELECT *` from that role fails loudly with a permission error.

subtopics.name: Trigger-based audit log: who, what, when, why on every tenant table
subtopics.learn: Design `audit_log (id bigint generated always as identity, tenant_id uuid, occurred_at timestamptz default clock_timestamp(), actor_id uuid, actor_role text, session_user_name text default session_user, application_name text, request_id text, table_name text, row_pk text, op text, old_row jsonb, new_row jsonb, changed_cols text[])` and one generic PL/pgSQL function attached with `CREATE TRIGGER audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON t FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_row()` that reads `TG_OP`, `TG_TABLE_NAME`, `to_jsonb(OLD)`, `to_jsonb(NEW)`, and the actor from `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)` and `current_setting('app.request_id', true)`. Strip or encrypt PII columns in `old_row`/`new_row` using the inventory from the classification step so the audit log does not become the least protected copy of the data. Use `AFTER` not `BEFORE` so a rolled-back statement leaves no audit row, and compute `changed_cols` from a jsonb diff so reviewers can filter for changes to sensitive fields.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: PL/pgSQL Trigger Functions (TG_OP, OLD, NEW)

subtopics.name: Making the audit trail append-only and tamper-evident; pgaudit for DDL and roles
subtopics.learn: Append-only means four things: `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE ON audit_log FROM PUBLIC, app_user` plus a `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE OR TRUNCATE` trigger that raises `EXCEPTION 'audit_log is append-only'` to cover the owner as well; RLS on `audit_log` so tenants read only their own entries; a `prev_hash bytea` chain (`digest(prev_hash || canonical_row_json, 'sha256')`) that lets an auditor detect a deleted or edited row; and periodic export of closed partitions to object storage with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. Application triggers cannot see `ALTER ROLE`, `GRANT`, `DROP TRIGGER` or a DBA at a psql prompt; enable the `pgaudit` extension with `pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role'` (and `read, write` on sensitive schemas via `pgaudit.role`) so those events land in the server log shipped to the SIEM, and document which events live in which log.

resource.label: pgaudit: PostgreSQL Audit Extension (GitHub, configuration reference)

subtopics.name: Retention, erasure and partitions: deleting without breaking the audit trail
subtopics.learn: Partition high-volume tables (`audit_log`, `llm_calls`, `messages`) by month with `PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at)` so retention is `DROP TABLE audit_log_2025_03` (instant, no bloat) rather than a `DELETE` that vacuums for hours; pre-create partitions from a scheduled job and test the 'no partition for this month' failure before it happens on a Sunday. Separate three deletion semantics and put each in the model doc: soft delete (`deleted_at` plus a RESTRICTIVE policy `deleted_at IS NULL` so hidden rows stay hidden from every query path), hard delete (row gone, audit rows remain but the PII inside them is pseudonymised by rewriting `actor_id` to a tombstone via a privileged job), and crypto-shred for tenant offboarding. State plainly that PITR backups retain data for the backup window and that any erasure SLA must include that window.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs: Table Partitioning (declarative range partitioning, detaching)

subtopics.name: Modelling AI-specific tables: conversations, llm_calls, tool_calls and embeddings under RLS
subtopics.learn: Design `conversations`, `messages`, `llm_calls` (model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, latency_ms, cost_usd, provider_request_id, `prompt_ref` pointing at redacted storage), `tool_calls` (name, arguments jsonb, result jsonb, approved_by) and `embeddings` (pgvector `vector(1536)` plus `source_table`, `source_id`, `tenant_id`) all carrying `tenant_id` and the same RLS policy; the vector table is the one people forget, and a `<->` nearest-neighbour query without tenant scoping returns another tenant's document chunks as context. Treat embeddings as derived PII (inversion attacks recover text) and tool `arguments`/`result` as free text with the highest classification of their inputs. Store raw prompts and completions in a short-TTL partition or as a hash plus a redacted copy, add `training_opt_out boolean` and `data_region text` on `tenants`, and make sure the LLM observability exporter (topic 54) reads from the masked view, never the base table.

resource.label: pgvector (GitHub README: indexing, filtering with WHERE, iterative scans)

subtopics.name: Writing the data model doc a client security team signs off
subtopics.learn: Structure the document the way reviewers read it: one data-flow diagram with trust boundaries (browser, API, worker, Postgres, KMS, LLM provider, object storage), a table of every store with its tenancy model and encryption layer, a threat list with the control that answers each one (IDOR across tenants -> RLS + composite FKs + test matrix; SQL injection -> parameterised queries + RLS as defence in depth; snapshot theft -> KMS volume + column encryption; insider DBA -> pgaudit + column encryption + no superuser app role; log leakage -> masked views + `log_statement` policy; backup retention -> stated PITR window + crypto-shred), and an evidence section linking to the CI output for the RLS matrix and catalog invariants. Map controls to the frameworks the client will cite (SOC 2 CC6.1 and CC6.7, ISO 27001 Annex A.8, GDPR Art. 32 and Art. 17) without claiming compliance, and end with the residual risks you are asking them to accept, because a doc with no residual risks is the one they do not believe.

outcomes: You can stand up DefenderMate's schema in a fresh Postgres 16 container and run an RLS test matrix (positive, negative, cross-tenant INSERT and UPDATE, unset tenant, owner-with-FORCE) generated from the catalog across every table in `public`, passing in CI in under 60 seconds; deliberately dropping one policy makes the suite fail naming that table.

You can explain, with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output captured as `app_user`, why a policy written as `(SELECT current_setting(...))` produces an InitPlan and why a non-LEAKPROOF function in the query turned an index scan into a sequential scan, then fix it without weakening the policy.

You can reproduce the PgBouncer transaction-pooling leak (session-level `SET app.tenant_id` visible on the next checkout) in an automated test, and show the `set_config(..., true)` fix turning it green.

You can encrypt a PII column with a per-tenant data key wrapped by a KEK, look rows up by HMAC blind index, rotate the KEK without touching rows, and crypto-shred one tenant so its rows fail to decrypt while every other tenant is unaffected.

You can show an `audit_log` where UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE fail for every role including the owner, each row carries actor, request id, `TG_OP` and a redacted jsonb diff, and a hash-chain verification query pinpoints a manually deleted row.
You can run one catalog query that lists any table missing `tenant_id`, RLS, FORCE or a policy, and the CI job fails with that list when a new migration forgets any of them.

You can walk a security reviewer through the model doc in 20 minutes and answer 'what stops your support engineer reading tenant B's chat logs' and 'what happens to my data in your backups after I churn' with the specific control, its limits and a link to the evidence.
failureModes: A support tool needed read-all-tenants access, so an engineer added a second PERMISSIVE policy `USING (true) TO app_user` instead of a separate role; because permissive policies are ORed, every API request could read every tenant, and it was found by a customer who saw another company's name in an autocomplete dropdown.

RLS was enabled but never FORCED, and the API connected as the table owner because the Terraform module reused the migration credentials; RLS applied to nobody for eight months and the first indication was a penetration tester swapping a UUID in a URL.

Session-level `SET app.tenant_id` behind PgBouncer in transaction mode: under load, connections were reused mid-request and roughly one in 400 requests ran as the previous request's tenant, surfacing as 'random' data-corruption tickets nobody could reproduce in staging, which had no pooler.

The pgvector table for RAG had no `tenant_id` column because it was created from a notebook, so nearest-neighbour retrieval pulled another tenant's contract clauses into a prompt; the model summarised them fluently and the leak was only visible in the LLM trace store weeks later.

pgcrypto keys were interpolated as string literals by the ORM, so every encryption key sat in `pg_stat_statements`, the slow-query log and the APM tool's query capture, meaning the column encryption protected against nothing the volume encryption did not already cover.

The audit trigger logged `to_jsonb(NEW)` for the users table including plaintext PII columns, so the audit log became the largest unencrypted copy of customer data in the system and was excluded from the encryption review because 'it's just logs'.

A GDPR erasure request was fulfilled with `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ...` while the audit log, the embeddings table and 35 days of PITR backups still held the data; the DPO found out when the same person's name appeared in a support search a month later.
interviewQuestions: A regulated customer wants to run our multi-tenant AI product but their security team says shared tables are unacceptable. Walk me through how you decide between arguing for pooled tables with RLS, moving them to a dedicated schema or database, and what evidence you bring to the meeting to change their mind or to concede gracefully.

Explain how a Postgres row-level security policy is actually evaluated inside a query, what USING versus WITH CHECK protect, how permissive and restrictive policies combine, and give me a concrete case where a correct-looking policy still leaks data.

We run the API behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode and set the tenant with `SET app.tenant_id` at the start of each request. Production shows occasional cross-tenant reads that never reproduce in staging. Debug it out loud, then tell me the fix and the test that proves the fix.

Design the encryption story for PII in a system where customers must be able to search by email, we must honour erasure requests within 30 days, and we keep 35 days of backups. Which layer encrypts what, where do the keys live, how does lookup work, and what exactly happens on an erasure request?

After enabling RLS, a dashboard query went from 40 ms to 6 seconds. The policy is `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` and the query filters on a user-defined function. What is happening in the planner, and how do you fix it without weakening the policy?

Design an append-only audit trail for a multi-tenant system that a SOC 2 auditor will accept. How do you make it immutable when the table owner can always drop a trigger, what do you deliberately keep out of it, and how would you prove to the auditor that nothing was deleted last quarter?

Our RAG pipeline stores document chunks and embeddings in pgvector. A customer asks whether another tenant could ever see their documents in a model answer. Give me the complete answer: the retrieval query, the storage model, the tests, and the residual risk you would disclose.
proofOfWork: A public repository containing DefenderMate's multi-tenant schema as versioned migrations (tenants, users, conversations, messages, llm_calls, tool_calls, embeddings, audit_log) with RLS enabled and forced on every table, composite tenant foreign keys, pgcrypto-encrypted PII columns with HMAC blind indexes, an envelope-encryption module with per-tenant data keys (a local KEK stub for CI, KMS in production), and a generic audit trigger with hash chaining and an append-only guard. The CI workflow spins up Postgres 16 behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, runs the catalog-generated RLS test matrix across every table, runs the catalog invariant queries, demonstrates the pooled-connection tenant leak failing before the `set_config` fix and passing after, and crypto-shreds one tenant while asserting the others still decrypt. Alongside the code sits a six-page security review document with a data-flow diagram, threat-to-control table, framework mapping, evidence links to the green CI run and a residual-risk section, written so a client CISO could sign it without a call.
